stars.label: The Map of Ideas
stars.title: The Map of Ideas
stars.body: A map where every idea sits next to the ideas it connects to.

stars.label: Gödel
stars.title: Gödel, 1931
stars.body:
In 1931 Gödel showed that a system of rules can be sound and still leave true things unproven, and that it cannot vouch for itself from within.

Everything nearby grows from that: what proof and truth are, what systems can and cannot reach, and where people have carried the idea since.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Gödel’s incompleteness theorems
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems
Gödel, K. (1931). Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze der Principia Mathematica und verwandter Systeme I. Monatshefte für Mathematik und Physik 38, 173–198.

stars.label: what it says
stars.title: What Gödel’s incompleteness theorems say
stars.body:
Take any set of rules for proving things in math, as long as the rules are clear enough that a computer could check a proof, and strong enough to do basic arithmetic. Gödel showed two things about such a system.

First, it cannot prove everything that is true. There are always true statements about numbers that the rules can never reach. Second, it cannot prove that it is itself consistent, meaning that it will never contradict itself.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Gödel’s incompleteness theorems
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems

stars.label: numbering trick
stars.title: Gödel numbering: statements become numbers
stars.body:
Gödel did not turn ordinary language into logic. He started with a small formal language (symbols like 0, +, ×, =, “for all”) and gave each symbol a number. A statement is a row of symbols, so it becomes one big number. A proof is a list of statements, so it gets a number the same way.

After that, “this number is a valid proof of that number” is a plain claim about numbers, which arithmetic can express. That is how math ends up talking about itself.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Gödel numbering

stars.label: primes in the trick
stars.title: Gödel numbering: where primes come in
stars.body:
The recipe for the big number uses primes. For a row of symbols with codes a, b, c you compute 2a × 3b × 5c, and so on along the row.

Every number breaks into primes in only one way, so you can always decode it back to the exact statement.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Gödel numbering

stars.label: the sentence
stars.title: The Gödel sentence that points at itself
stars.body:
With that machinery Gödel built a sentence that says, in effect, “this sentence cannot be proven in this system”. Now ask whether the system can prove it.

If it proves the sentence, then the sentence is false (it said it can’t be proven), so the system just proved something false and is broken. If it cannot prove it, then the sentence is true, because that is exactly what it claims. A system that isn’t broken is stuck with the second option: there is a true statement it cannot reach.

stars.label: second theorem
stars.title: Gödel’s second theorem
stars.body:
The reasoning “if the system is consistent, the sentence can’t be proven” can itself be written down inside the system. So the system can prove: “if I’m consistent, then the Gödel sentence is true”.

Now suppose it could also prove “I am consistent”. It could combine the two and prove the Gödel sentence. But we just saw it cannot, unless it is broken. So it cannot prove its own consistency either.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems
Wikipedia: Gödel’s incompleteness theorems

stars.label: the conditions
stars.title: The conditions a system must meet for Gödel’s theorems to apply
stars.body:
The theorem is conditional. It needs rules that a computer can check, enough arithmetic (addition and multiplication together), and consistency. It says nothing about systems that fail these.

Every use of the theorem outside mathematics has to show that its system meets all three.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems

stars.label: weakest condition?
stars.title: Which of the three conditions is the weakest link when the theorem is applied to minds?
stars.body: The theorem needs rules a computer can check, enough arithmetic, and consistency. For a mind, each of the three is a claim someone has to defend.

stars.label: seen from outside
stars.title: Who sees from outside that the Gödel sentence is true
stars.body:
The system cannot prove the sentence. We can see that it is true, but only from outside, by reasoning about the system. Inside, it is unprovable. Outside, we see it is true precisely because it is unprovable.

That gap between true and provable inside is the whole theorem.

stars.label: what true means
stars.title: What true means in Gödel’s setting
stars.body:
True means true of the actual natural numbers, 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. A statement like “there are infinitely many primes” is true if it holds for those numbers, whether or not anyone can prove it. Truth is the numbers themselves, and a proof is one way of getting at them.

This assumes the numbers are a definite thing that exists independently of our rulebooks. Some accept that (Gödel did). A formalist would say math is only the rules, so “true” means “provable”, and the Gödel sentence is neither true nor false, just undecidable.

sources.t: Wikipedia: True arithmetic

stars.label: three words
stars.title: Provable, true, consistent
stars.body: Provable is about one statement: the system can derive it from its rules. True is about one statement: it is correct about the actual numbers. Consistent is about the whole system: it never proves a statement and also its opposite.

stars.label: the judge
stars.title: The judge picture of proof and truth
stars.body:
Provable is “the judge ruled on it”. True is “the ruling matches what actually happened”. Consistent is “the judge never issues two contradictory rulings”.

A judge can be consistent and still wrong, because never contradicting yourself does not mean you are right. Consistency is the weakest of the three. It only says the system does not blow up.

stars.label: complete, incomplete
stars.title: Complete and incomplete
stars.body:
Complete means every statement you can write in the system’s language gets settled: either the statement or its opposite can be proven. Incomplete means at least one statement exists where the system can prove neither it nor its opposite.

So incomplete just means there is at least one statement the system cannot prove (and cannot disprove). Most statements, primes included, are settled in the normal way.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Completeness (logic)

stars.label: free certainty
stars.title: Why a broken system proves “I am consistent”
stars.body: An inconsistent system proves everything, true and false alike, including “I am consistent”. So a proof of consistency from inside is worth nothing. A healthy system cannot give one, and a broken one gives it for free.

stars.label: trust
stars.title: Trust: what a system can have instead of proof
stars.body:
A system that has run for a long time without a contradiction has good reason to expect it is consistent. Mathematicians trust arithmetic this way: nobody has found a contradiction in centuries, and a stronger system proves it consistent.

It is trust built from outside or from experience, never certainty from inside.

stars.label: proof or trust?
stars.title: Is trust built from experience a different kind of knowing than proof?
stars.body: Mathematicians trust arithmetic because nobody has found a contradiction in centuries. That is evidence of a different kind than a proof, and it is the only kind a system can have about itself.

stars.label: Tarski
stars.title: Tarski: a system cannot define its own truth
stars.body: Inside the machine you can build “provable”, but you cannot build “true”. Truth always has to be judged from a stronger place outside.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Tarski’s undefinability theorem
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Tarski’s Truth Definitions

stars.label: outside is trust
stars.title: Seeing from outside is a leap of trust
stars.body: What we actually do when we say the Gödel sentence is true is assume the system is consistent. That assumption is an act of trust. It is no view from above.

stars.label: what a system is
stars.title: What a formal system is
stars.body:
A system is a rulebook with two parts: a starting list of statements accepted without proof (axioms, like “every number has a next number”), and rules for deriving new statements from old ones. A proof is a chain of steps from the axioms using only those rules.

The standard system for numbers is called Peano arithmetic.

stars.label: primes: provable
stars.title: Primes are provable, so where is the unprovable part?
stars.body:
The system proves that there are infinitely many primes, since Euclid’s argument can be written inside it. Gödel does not say everything is unprovable. Peano arithmetic covers addition, multiplication, ordering, divisibility and primes, and primes are only one thing it can talk about.

The unprovable statements are of two kinds. One is the Gödel sentence, which looks like an ordinary claim about numbers but is built so that its meaning points back at itself. The other is natural examples, like Goodstein’s theorem: you rewrite a number in a special way, subtract 1, bump the base, and repeat. It is true that the sequence always ends at 0, and ordinary arithmetic cannot prove it. So incompleteness lives at the edges of everyday math.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Euclid’s theorem

stars.label: Skolem, only ×
stars.title: A system based only on primes: Skolem arithmetic
stars.body:
This is the theory of whole numbers with multiplication only, no addition. Every number is a unique bundle of primes (12 = 2·2·3), so multiplication means “combine the bundles”. In that world you can talk about primes, divisibility and “infinitely many primes” with no trouble.

It is complete: every statement it can express is provable or disprovable, and a computer can even decide which. Gödel does not touch it. Addition alone (Presburger arithmetic) is also complete.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Presburger arithmetic (the addition-only sibling)

stars.label: why it is safe
stars.title: Why Gödel has nothing to grab there
stars.body:
Gödel’s theorem has a condition: the system must be strong enough to talk about itself. To build the self-pointing sentence, a system has to turn statements and proofs into numbers and say things like “this number encodes a valid proof of that number”. Checking a proof mixes addition and multiplication together. With only one of them the system cannot express that, so it cannot build the sentence.

It is like the robot that explodes when told “this sentence is false”. A robot with no way to understand self-reference cannot be tricked that way. The price is that the system is safe because it is weak.

stars.label: the threshold
stars.title: The threshold where Gödel’s theorems begin to apply
stars.body: Put addition and multiplication together and you are over it. Peano arithmetic and set theory both are. Above the threshold a system can describe itself and gets a blind spot. Below it the system is safe but can say little. Self-reference and incompleteness come as a package.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Peano axioms

stars.label: Goldbach
stars.title: Where primes meet addition
stars.body: The trouble returns where primes meet addition. Goldbach’s conjecture (every even number is a sum of two primes) mixes the two worlds, and that is where things get hard. Whether it is provable is open.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Goldbach’s conjecture

stars.label: programs
stars.title: Programs have the same shape
stars.body: Any programming language powerful enough to run arbitrary code can write programs that print their own source or inspect themselves. That is self-reference in a concrete form, and it is also why no program can check every other program for bugs. That is Turing’s version of Gödel.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Quine (computing)

stars.label: fixed means checkable
stars.title: What “fixed” means
stars.body: “Fixed” means a computer could check it: at any moment there is a clear list of rules and a mechanical way to tell whether a proof follows them. It does not mean the rules never change. A system that keeps changing is a sequence of fixed systems, each with its own blind spot.

stars.label: a rule for rules
stars.title: The rule for changing the rules is a rule
stars.body:
If the system changes its rules by a fixed procedure, like “whenever you find a Gödel sentence, add it as a new axiom”, the whole thing is just one bigger fixed system. Gödel applies to that bigger system.

The theorem only stops applying if the changes come from something that is not a mechanical procedure: a person’s free choice, an oracle, something non-computable.

stars.label: random changes
stars.title: Random changes
stars.body:
Once the coin has been flipped and the rule added, that snapshot is just another fixed system. A coin also cannot repair the gap, because nothing steers it toward true statements. It has no access to truth.

There is one subtle exception: an infinite stream of truly random choices is, with probability 1, not computable, so the system as a whole would not be a program. But that is escape by accident. You would get a system no one can check or use, with no guarantee it contains the truths you care about.

stars.label: unchecked system
stars.title: A system nobody can check at all
stars.body:
Then Gödel stops applying, because the theorem needs a system whose proofs a computer can check. Such a system can even be complete: flip a coin for every statement, “add it” or “add its opposite”, and you end up with a rulebook that settles everything.

But it would settle about half of the statements wrongly. It could be perfectly consistent and still “prove” false things about numbers. Complete is not the same as true.

stars.label: the triangle
stars.title: The triangle: checkable, complete, true
stars.body:
There is one special system that is complete and fully true: take every true statement about numbers as an axiom. It exists, but nobody can write it down or check it, so it is useless as a rulebook.

Gödel says no system can have all three. Pure randomness gives up checkability and truth, and only gets completeness by luck.

sources.t: Wikipedia: True arithmetic

stars.label: what escape takes
stars.title: What escaping would take
stars.body: Two things: the rule-changing cannot be mechanical, and it has to be connected to truth somehow. A person with real insight, or an oracle, might do both. A coin only does the first.

stars.label: checkable or not
stars.title: Checkable or uncheckable mechanics
stars.body:
If the mechanics are checkable (physics is computable and the brain follows fixed rules), the theorem has something to grab. Any rule-following mind would have true statements about itself that it cannot establish from inside, and it would take its own soundness on faith.

If they are uncheckable, say consciousness depends on something non-computable (Penrose’s bet), the theorem does not apply. Either way someone still has to show that a mind’s reasoning contains arithmetic in the relevant sense.

stars.label: the ladder
stars.title: Is there an ultimate outside? The ladder of systems
stars.body: Each outside is just a stronger system, and that system has its own blind spot, which needs an even stronger one to see. Logicians have studied this ladder (Tarski’s hierarchy, the progressions of theories by Turing and Feferman). It has no top. You just make the observer bigger.

stars.label: three views
stars.title: Three ways to take the ladder
stars.body:
Platonism: the top is the actual numbers, which exist apart from any rulebook. The cost is explaining how minds ever reach them.

No top: the ladder keeps going, and “true” always means true relative to some level.

The universe as the biggest system: if reality is the whole, nothing is outside it. Then either reality is not a formal system, or nobody inside can know all its truths.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Platonism in the Philosophy of Mathematics

stars.label: closed loops
stars.title: Closed systems: what a loop costs
stars.body:
If the top level loops back to the bottom, the system effectively vouches for its own consistency, and the second theorem says a consistent system cannot do that. So a closed loop has to give up one of three things.

Consistency: Priest and the dialetheists accept some true contradictions. Total truth: Kripke’s theory lets a system talk about its own truth, but sentences like the liar stay neither true nor false. The ladder itself: Aczel’s non-well-founded sets contain themselves.

Hofstadter’s tangled hierarchy is the intuitive version: you climb levels and end up where you started. The Gödel sentence is already a tiny closed loop, one step long.

sources.t: Kripke, S. (1975). Outline of a Theory of Truth. Journal of Philosophy 72(19), 690–716.

stars.label: any top?
stars.title: Is there an ultimate outside, or does the ladder go on forever?
stars.body: Each outside is a stronger system. Platonism says the top is the numbers themselves. The ladder view says there is no top.

stars.label: which cost?
stars.title: Contradictions or holes: which cost would you rather pay?
stars.body: A closed loop gives up consistency (dialetheism), total truth (Kripke’s holes) or the ladder itself (non-well-founded sets).

sources.t: Kripke, S. (1975). Outline of a Theory of Truth. Journal of Philosophy 72(19), 690–716.

stars.label: Hofstadter
stars.title: Hofstadter’s opposite reading: the loop is the self
stars.body: Hofstadter (Gödel, Escher, Bach and I Am a Strange Loop) says self-reference is where a self comes from, so the loop is the feature and no limit.

sources.t: Hofstadter, D. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books.
Hofstadter, D. (2007). I Am a Strange Loop. Basic Books.

stars.label: knows its hole
stars.title: A system that knows it is incomplete
stars.body:
A strong enough system can prove “if I’m consistent, there is a true statement I can’t prove”. So it can know it has a blind spot, but it can never point to what is in it, and it cannot be sure it is consistent either. That is Socrates in formal dress: it knows that it doesn’t know, but not what it doesn’t know.

The idea that such a system may be another level of consciousness has exactly this shape.

stars.label: mind contradicts
stars.title: A consistent mechanism can make contradictory minds
stars.body: People contradict themselves all the time, which looks like a reason to say a mind is not a consistent rulebook. That objection is weaker than it sounds. A perfectly consistent program can print “yes” on one screen and “no” on another. Gödel applies to the rules underneath, not to what comes out.

stars.label: Lucas, Penrose
stars.title: The “minds beat machines” side
stars.body: J. R. Lucas (1961) made the original argument, and Penrose (1989, 1994) sharpened it: we can see that the Gödel sentence is true, so we are not a fixed rulebook.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Penrose–Lucas argument
Lucas, J. R. (1961). Minds, Machines and Gödel. Philosophy 36(137), 112–127.
Penrose, R. (1989). The Emperor’s New Mind. Oxford University Press.

stars.label: the replies
stars.title: Replies to the Lucas–Penrose argument
stars.body: Benacerraf and Putnam made the point that we only see the sentence is true if we assume the system is consistent, and nobody can certify that about their own mind from inside. So we have the same blind spot as the machine. Chalmers and Feferman wrote detailed critiques of Penrose along the same lines.

sources.t: Benacerraf, P. (1967). God, the Devil, and Gödel. The Monist 51(1), 9–32.
Putnam, H. (1960). Minds and Machines. In S. Hook (ed.), Dimensions of Mind. New York University Press.
Chalmers, D. (1995). Minds, machines, and mathematics. PSYCHE 2(9).
Feferman, S. (1995). Penrose’s Gödelian argument. PSYCHE 2(7).

stars.label: Gödel’s view
stars.title: Gödel’s own view
stars.body: He gave a disjunction: either the mind outruns any machine, or there are math problems that are absolutely unsolvable. He would not say which. It is more careful than Lucas and Penrose.

sources.t: Gödel, K. (1951). Some basic theorems on the foundations of mathematics and their implications (Gibbs Lecture). In Collected Works, Vol. III.

stars.label: non-computable mind?
stars.title: Is anything non-computable involved in a mind?
stars.body: A mind that depends on something non-computable would escape the theorem. So far there is no evidence either way.

stars.label: is it arithmetic?
stars.title: Does a mind’s reasoning contain arithmetic in the relevant sense?
stars.body: The theorem needs a system with enough arithmetic. People do arithmetic, which makes it plausible, and it has not been shown for the reasoning inside a brain.

stars.label: a test for claims
stars.title: A test for these claims
stars.body:
Can the person say what the theorem assumes, and show that their system meets it? Consciousness is a field where big words (Gödel, topology, Kleene) get borrowed as analogies much faster than anyone checks the conditions.

“Ambition getting ahead of rigor” is common and forgivable. The danger starts when it is published as if the rigor were already there.

stars.label: theorist inside?
stars.title: What would a model look like where the theorist is inside the system being modeled?
stars.body: The observer who builds a theory is inside the loop too. A model that includes that observer does not exist yet.

stars.label: quantum bridge
stars.title: Quantum mechanics and uncertainty
stars.body:
The uncertainty principle is a physical limit: a particle does not have a sharp position and momentum at the same time. Gödel is a logical limit on formal systems. They are limits of different kinds that share one lesson, that a complete, fully determined description does not exist. Both broke an early-1900s dream (Laplace’s predictable universe, Hilbert’s complete mathematics).

There is one real bridge. In 2015, Cubitt, Perez-Garcia and Wolf showed that for certain quantum materials, whether the system has an energy gap is undecidable. Other links, like Penrose’s, are speculation that most logicians reject.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Uncertainty principle

stars.label: reaches reality?
stars.title: Does the theorem say anything about reality?
stars.body:
Gödel’s theorem is conditional: if a system has fixed rules and can do arithmetic, then it has true statements it cannot prove. To say anything about reality, you first have to assume reality (or the mind) is such a system, and the theorem cannot give you that assumption.

Even if you grant it, it is a statement about maps, not territory. If physics were fully described by one formal theory, the theory would have unprovable truths, but reality would keep doing what it does. Incompleteness would limit what we can derive, not what exists.

stars.label: gluing obstruction
stars.title: Gluing obstructions
stars.body: Local pieces that each make sense but cannot be stitched into one global picture. It is a cousin of Gödel’s flavor (local provability against global truth), and unlike loose talk of an “inverted Gödel” it can be made precise. It is a promising place to look for results that connect self-reference and physics or mind.

sources.t: Cubitt, T. S., Perez-Garcia, D., Wolf, M. M. (2015). Undecidability of the spectral gap. Nature 528, 207–211.

stars.label: gluing for self?
stars.title: Is there a precise version of a gluing obstruction for self-models?
stars.body: Local pieces that cannot be glued into a global picture are mathematically precise. Whether they describe how a self-model fails is open.

stars.label: a threshold in nature?
stars.title: Is there a threshold of self-reference in physical or biological systems?
stars.body: Gödel needs addition and multiplication together. Whether physical or biological systems have an equivalent point where they start to model themselves is open.

stars.label: numbers out there?
stars.title: Are numbers out there, or rules we invented?
stars.body: Platonists say numbers exist apart from any rulebook, and Gödel believed this. Formalists say math is only the rules we wrote down.

sources.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Platonism in the Philosophy of Mathematics

stars.label: the asymmetry
stars.title: The asymmetry between doubt and certainty in a system
stars.body: A broken system can be certain of itself for free, while a healthy one can only trust. So from inside, total certainty is what a broken mind would feel, and a bit of doubt is what a sound one would carry. That would make humility a structural feature, and a virtue only second.

stars.label: Löb’s theorem
stars.title: Löb’s theorem makes it rigorous
stars.body:
Take a system T that is strong enough to talk about itself, and read its theorems as its beliefs. Löb (1955) says that if T proves “if I prove P, then P is true”, then T proves P outright. So a system that trusts itself about a statement ends up asserting that statement, whether or not it is true. Gödel’s second theorem is the special case where P is a falsehood.

That gives a precise version of arrogance: blanket self-trust, “whatever I conclude is true”, is something only a broken system can have. That is a theorem, not a metaphor.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Löb’s theorem
Löb, M. H. (1955). Solution of a problem of Leon Henkin. Journal of Symbolic Logic 20(2), 115–118.

stars.label: escape routes
stars.title: Escape routes from Löb’s theorem that match the intuition of humility
stars.body: Partial trust: you trust yourself for restricted classes of statements. Trust the level below: Feferman’s progressions, where each system vouches for the previous one but not for itself. Probabilistic self-trust: work attributed to Christiano and colleagues says a probabilistic version can talk about its own reliability if it allows a small margin of error. Certainty breaks it, and calibrated doubt does not. verify

sources.t: Feferman, S. (1962). Transfinite recursive progressions of axiomatic theories. Journal of Symbolic Logic 27(3), 259–316.

stars.label: the AI version
stars.title: The AI safety version
stars.body: An AI that wants to approve a successor as strong as itself runs into Löb. People call it the Löbian obstacle (Yudkowsky and Herreshoff). verify

sources.t: Yudkowsky, E., Herreshoff, M. (2013). Tiling Agents for Self-Modifying AI, and the Löbian Obstacle. MIRI technical report.

stars.label: what stays open
stars.title: What stays open
stars.body: To make it rigorous for minds or governments, someone has to write down a formal model: an agent is a theory, and its beliefs are its theorems. Inside that model the arrogance result is exact. Whether real minds or institutions fit the model is a separate claim.

stars.label: who said it
stars.title: Who said something like it before and around Gödel
stars.body:
Jacob Bronowski, in The Ascent of Man (the episode “Knowledge or Certainty”), uses Gödel and Heisenberg to argue that no knowledge is absolute, and that people who claim absolute certainty act as if they had the knowledge of gods. verify the wording

Without Gödel: Russell’s remark that fools and fanatics are certain while wiser people are full of doubt (paraphrased from memory). verify Cromwell’s plea to the Church of Scotland: “think it possible you may be mistaken”. Popper’s fallibilism and The Open Society. Hayek’s argument that no central planner can hold all the knowledge. The overconfidence research (Dunning-Kruger) shows that certainty and accuracy are only loosely connected.

sources.t: Bronowski, J. (1973). The Ascent of Man, episode 11, “Knowledge or Certainty”. BBC.

stars.label: the caution
stars.title: The caution against over-reading Gödel’s theorems
stars.body: Torkel Franzén, and Sokal and Bricmont (Fashionable Nonsense), point out that Gödel gets borrowed for politics and society much more than it can support. The humility argument stands on its own, and Gödel works as an image for it. The trick that “a broken system certifies itself for free” is a neat structural parallel, and I haven’t seen it made rigorously for minds or governments.

sources.t: Franzén, T. (2005). Gödel’s Theorem: An Incomplete Guide to Its Use and Abuse. A K Peters.
Sokal, A., Bricmont, J. (1998). Fashionable Nonsense. Picador.

stars.label: what is a belief?
stars.title: What counts as a belief in the formal model of an agent?
stars.body: In Löb’s setting an agent is a theory and its beliefs are its theorems. Real minds may fit that badly.

stars.label: calibrated doubt?
stars.title: Does “calibrated doubt keeps a system sound” have a precise form for AI models?
stars.body: A probabilistic version of self-trust seems to survive if it allows a margin of error. How far that reaches for AI models is open.

stars.label: broken signature
stars.title: The signature of a broken system in society
stars.body: A system that declares itself complete and certain, like an ideology with an answer for everything or a power that answers to nobody, has the signature of the broken machine: it certifies itself for free.

stars.label: outside built in
stars.title: Building the outside in
stars.body: Healthy systems build the outside in: courts, a free press, elections, an opposition, ways to amend the rules. Each is a view from a level above the one in charge, and each has its own blind spot, so you need several.

stars.label: Constitution
stars.title: Gödel and the US Constitution
stars.body: Gödel reportedly found a loophole in the US Constitution that could allow a dictatorship. It fits the picture, since a rulebook cannot fully protect itself from within. verify

sources.t: Wikipedia: Kurt Gödel

stars.label: argument, no theorem
stars.title: Argument, not theorem
stars.body: The political version is different from the math one, because you can argue it and cannot prove it. A stricter claim, that any system that cannot be questioned from outside will drift, is empirical and comes from outside Gödel. Social choice theory and models of fallibilism are more honest tools here.

stars.label: designed or emergent?
stars.title: Does a system’s self-doubt have to be designed in, or can it emerge?
stars.body: Courts and a free press were designed. Whether doubt can grow inside a system without anyone building it is the question.

stars.label: Franzén
stars.title: Torkel Franzén, Gödel’s Theorem: An Incomplete Guide to Its Use and Abuse
stars.body: The sober guide to what the theorem can and cannot be used for. Start here.

sources.t: Franzén, T. (2005). Gödel’s Theorem: An Incomplete Guide to Its Use and Abuse. A K Peters.

stars.label: Hofstadter
stars.title: Douglas Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach and I Am a Strange Loop
stars.body: The MIU puzzle, tangled hierarchies, and the self as a loop.

sources.t: Hofstadter, D. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books.
Hofstadter, D. (2007). I Am a Strange Loop. Basic Books.

stars.label: Lucas, Penrose
stars.title: J. R. Lucas (1961) and Roger Penrose (1989, 1994)
stars.body: The argument that minds outrun machines: “Minds, Machines and Gödel”, The Emperor’s New Mind, Shadows of the Mind.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Penrose–Lucas argument
Lucas, J. R. (1961). Minds, Machines and Gödel. Philosophy 36(137), 112–127.
Penrose, R. (1989). The Emperor’s New Mind. Oxford University Press.
Penrose, R. (1994). Shadows of the Mind. Oxford University Press.

stars.label: the replies
